content: Natural oil polyols (NOPs), also referred to as NOPs, are polyols that are synthesized from vegetable oils through various chemical processes. These materials are primarily utilized in the production of polyurethanes. Most NOPs are classified as biobased products, as defined by the United States Secretary of Agriculture under the Farm Security and Rural Investment Act of 2002. While NOPs share common sources and applications, their chemical properties can vary significantly depending on the specific production methods employed. All NOPs are clear liquids, with colors ranging from colorless to medium yellow. Their viscosity is variable and is influenced by the molecular weight and the average number of hydroxyl groups per molecule. Higher molecular weight and greater hydroxyl content both contribute to increased viscosity. Odor is another important characteristic of NOPs, and it varies between different types of NOPs. Chemically, most NOPs remain similar to their parent vegetable oils, which makes them susceptible to rancidity. This occurs due to the autoxidation of fatty acid chains containing carbon-carbon double bonds, leading to the formation of odorous, low molecular weight aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids. The presence of odor is undesirable not only in the NOPs themselves but also in the materials manufactured from them. There are only a limited number of naturally occurring vegetable oils (triglycerides) that contain unreacted hydroxyl groups, which are responsible for the reactivity and naming of these polyols. Castor oil is the only commercially available natural oil polyol that is directly derived from a plant source. All other NOPs require chemical modification of plant-derived oils. The use of renewable resources as feedstocks for chemical processes is intended to reduce reliance on non-renewable fossil fuels and decrease the overall production of carbon dioxide, a major greenhouse gas. It has been estimated that the production of NOPs results in 36% lower global warming emissions (carbon dioxide), a 61% reduction in non-renewable energy use, and a 23% reduction in total energy demand compared to polyols derived from petrochemicals. Approximately 90% of the fatty acids in castor oil consist of ricinoleic acid, which contains a hydroxyl group on the 12th carbon and a carbon-carbon double bond. The primary component of castor oil is a tri-ester of ricinoleic acid and glycerin. Other vegetable oils, such as soybean oil, peanut oil, and canola oil, contain carbon-carbon double bonds but lack hydroxyl groups. Various processes are employed to introduce hydroxyl groups onto the carbon chains of fatty acids, most of which involve oxidation of the carbon-carbon double bonds. For example, treating vegetable oils with ozone cleaves the double bonds, producing esters or alcohols depending on the processing conditions. Air oxidation (autoxidation), which is the chemical process involved in the drying of drying oils, increases molecular weight and introduces hydroxyl groups. The radical reactions involved in autoxidation can produce a complex mixture of crosslinked and oxidized triglycerides. Treating vegetable oils with peroxy acids generates epoxides, which can react with nucleophiles to form hydroxyl groups. This can be achieved in a single-step process. Additionally, unsaturated triglycerides or methyl esters of fatty acids can undergo hydroformylation reactions, where carbon monoxide and hydrogen are used in the presence of a metal catalyst to add formyl (-CHO) groups to the chain, followed by hydrogenation to produce hydroxyl groups. Castor oil has numerous applications, many of which are attributed to the presence of the hydroxyl group. This functional group allows for chemical derivatization of the oil and modifies its properties compared to vegetable oils that lack hydroxyl groups. Castor oil undergoes most reactions typical of alcohols, with its most industrially significant reaction being with diisocyanates to produce polyurethanes. Castor oil has been used to manufacture a variety of polyurethane products, including coatings and foams, and its derivatives continue to be an area of active development. For instance, castor oil derivatized with propylene oxide is used to produce polyurethane foam for mattresses, while other derivatives are employed in coatings. Beyond castor oil, which is relatively expensive and not domestically produced in many industrialized countries, the use of polyols derived from vegetable oils for polyurethane production began gaining attention around 2004. One prominent advocate for these polyurethanes is the Ford Motor Company, which announced plans to use polyurethane foam made from NOPs in the seats of its 2008 Ford Mustang. NOPs are also being utilized in polyurethane slab foam for conventional and memory foam mattresses. One of the earliest applications of NOPs (excluding castor oil) was in the production of spray-on polyurethane foam insulation for buildings.
